claim: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is caused by diminished Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein.
source: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is caused by diminished Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein, leading to neuromuscular junction (NMJ) dysfunction and spinal motor neuron (MN) loss.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of SMA research and is cited in the introduction with references to Lefebvre et al., 1995.

claim: Diminished SMN protein leads to neuromuscular junction (NMJ) dysfunction.
source: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is caused by diminished Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein, leading to neuromuscular junction (NMJ) dysfunction and spinal motor neuron (MN) loss.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in SMA research supported by multiple studies.

claim: Diminished SMN protein leads to spinal motor neuron (MN) loss.
source: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is caused by diminished Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein, leading to neuromuscular junction (NMJ) dysfunction and spinal motor neuron (MN) loss.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in SMA research supported by multiple studies.

claim: Loss of the C. elegans SMN ortholog, SMN-1, causes NMJ defects.
source: Loss of the C. elegans SMN ortholog, SMN-1, causes NMJ defects.
evidence: This is supported by previous research cited in the manuscript (Briese et al., 2009).

claim: Increased levels of the C. elegans Gemin3 ortholog, MEL-46, ameliorates NMJ defects in smn-1(lf) animals.
source: We found that increased levels of the C. elegans Gemin3 ortholog, MEL-46, ameliorates these defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2, including aldicarb response and synaptic protein localization assays.

claim: Increased MEL-46 levels restored perturbed microRNA (miR-2) function in smn-1(lf) animals.
source: Increased MEL-46 levels also restored perturbed microRNA (miR-2) function in smn-1(lf) animals.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing GFP reporter expression and miR-2 levels.

claim: miR-2 regulates expression of the C. elegans M2 muscarinic receptor (m2R) ortholog, GAR-2.
source: We determined that miR-2 regulates expression of the C. elegans M2 muscarinic receptor (m2R) ortholog, GAR-2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP reporter assays, CRISPR experiments, and genetic suppression studies shown in Figure 4.

claim: GAR-2 loss ameliorated smn-1(lf) synaptic defects.
source: GAR-2 loss ameliorated smn-1(lf) and mel-46(lf) synaptic defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assays and synaptic protein localization studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: GAR-2 loss ameliorated mel-46(lf) synaptic defects.
source: GAR-2 loss ameliorated smn-1(lf) and mel-46(lf) synaptic defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In an SMA mouse model, m2R levels were increased.
source: In an SMA mouse model, m2R levels were increased and pharmacological inhibition of m2R rescued MN process defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of m2R rescued MN process defects in an SMA mouse model.
source: In an SMA mouse model, m2R levels were increased and pharmacological inhibition of m2R rescued MN process defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by axon length measurements after methoctramine treatment shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Decreased SMN leads to defective microRNA function via MEL-46 misregulation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest decreased SMN leads to defective microRNA function via MEL-46 misregulation, followed by increased m2R expression, and neuronal dysfunction in SMA.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of multiple experiments showing MEL-46 mislocalization, decreased miR-2 levels, and rescue by MEL-46 overexpression.

claim: Decreased SMN leads to increased m2R expression.
source: Collectively, these results suggest decreased SMN leads to defective microRNA function via MEL-46 misregulation, followed by increased m2R expression, and neuronal dysfunction in SMA.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased m2R levels in SMA mouse motor neurons and increased GAR-2 translation in smn-1(lf) animals.

claim: Decreased SMN leads to neuronal dysfunction in SMA.
source: Collectively, these results suggest decreased SMN leads to defective microRNA function via MEL-46 misregulation, followed by increased m2R expression, and neuronal dysfunction in SMA.
evidence: This is supported by the observed NMJ defects, synaptic protein mislocalization, and axon outgrowth defects in SMA models.

claim: SMA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease.
source: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease and the leading genetic cause of infant death in the US (Cusin et al., 2003; Pearn, 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by cited references.

claim: SMA is the leading genetic cause of infant death in the US.
source: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease and the leading genetic cause of infant death in the US (Cusin et al., 2003; Pearn, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by cited epidemiological studies.

claim: SMA is caused by homozygous deletion or mutation of the SMN1 gene.
source: SMA is caused by homozygous deletion or mutation of the SMN1 (Survival Motor Neuron 1) gene, resulting in reduced Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein levels (Lefebvre et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Homozygous deletion or mutation of the SMN1 gene results in reduced SMN protein levels.
source: SMA is caused by homozygous deletion or mutation of the SMN1 (Survival Motor Neuron 1) gene, resulting in reduced Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein levels (Lefebvre et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: SMN expression is ubiquitous.
source: SMN expression is ubiquitous, but particularly essential for motor neuron survival (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: SMN is particularly essential for motor neuron survival.
source: SMN expression is ubiquitous, but particularly essential for motor neuron survival (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Disease severity in SMA correlates with the extent of SMN loss.
source: Disease severity, as well as spinal cord α-MN dysfunction and degeneration, correlates with the extent of SMN loss (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Spinal cord α-MN dysfunction correlates with the extent of SMN loss.
source: Disease severity, as well as spinal cord α-MN dysfunction and degeneration, correlates with the extent of SMN loss (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Spinal cord α-MN degeneration correlates with the extent of SMN loss.
source: Disease severity, as well as spinal cord α-MN dysfunction and degeneration, correlates with the extent of SMN loss (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: SMN is conserved across species.
source: SMN is conserved across species (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: SMN plays a role in snRNP assembly.
source: Studies of various SMA models suggest a role for SMN in several cellular processes including snRNP assembly (Golembe et al., 2005; Yong et al., 2002), messenger RNA (mRNA) transport (Fallini et al., 2011), and local translation (Dimitriadi et al., 2010; Kye et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: SMN plays a role in messenger RNA (mRNA) transport.
source: Studies of various SMA models suggest a role for SMN in several cellular processes including snRNP assembly (Golembe et al., 2005; Yong et al., 2002), messenger RNA (mRNA) transport (Fallini et al., 2011), and local translation (Dimitriadi et al., 2010; Kye et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: SMN plays a role in local translation.
source: Studies of various SMA models suggest a role for SMN in several cellular processes including snRNP assembly (Golembe et al., 2005; Yong et al., 2002), messenger RNA (mRNA) transport (Fallini et al., 2011), and local translation (Dimitriadi et al., 2010; Kye et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: SMN function has not been linked definitively to MN degeneration caused by SMN loss.
source: SMN function, however, has not been linked definitively to MN degeneration or synaptic transmission defects caused by SMN loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: SMN function has not been linked definitively to synaptic transmission defects caused by SMN loss.
source: SMN function, however, has not been linked definitively to MN degeneration or synaptic transmission defects caused by SMN loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: microRNAs (miRNAs) often repress protein translation by binding to the 3'UTR of mRNA targets.
source: microRNAs (miRNAs) are non-coding RNAs that often repress protein translation, by a mechanism that requires miRNA binding to the 3'UTR of mRNA targets.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA function.

claim: Disruption of the miRNA pathway in spinal MNs leads to severe degeneration.
source: Disruption of the miRNA pathway in spinal MNs leads to severe degeneration (Haramati et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: SMN loss alters levels and/or activity of specific miRNAs.
source: SMN loss alters levels and/or activity of specific miRNAs (Haramati et al., 2010; Kye et al., 2014; Valsecchi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014), but the cellular mechanisms leading to altered miRNA expression and/or function are unknown.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The cellular mechanisms leading to altered miRNA expression and/or function due to SMN loss are unknown.
source: SMN loss alters levels and/or activity of specific miRNAs (Haramati et al., 2010; Kye et al., 2014; Valsecchi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014), but the cellular mechanisms leading to altered miRNA expression and/or function are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: The RNA helicase Gemin3 associates with SMN.
source: The RNA helicase Gemin3 associates with both SMN and RNA-induced silencing complex components (Charroux et al., 1999; Höck et al., 2007; Hutvágner and Zamore, 2002; Meister et al., 2005; Mourelatos et al., 2002; Murashov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The RNA helicase Gemin3 associates with RNA-induced silencing complex components.
source: The RNA helicase Gemin3 associates with both SMN and RNA-induced silencing complex components (Charroux et al., 1999; Höck et al., 2007; Hutvágner and Zamore, 2002; Meister et al., 2005; Mourelatos et al., 2002; Murashov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Gemin3 and SMN levels decrease concomitantly.
source: Gemin3 and SMN levels decrease concomitantly, suggestive of a functional link (Feng et al., 2005; Helmken et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: SMN1, Gemin3, and multiple miRNA pathway components are conserved in C. elegans.
source: SMN1, Gemin3, and multiple miRNA pathway components are conserved in C. elegans (Grishok et al., 2001; Miguel-Aliaga et al., 1999; Minasaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in smn-1 cause behavioral abnormalities in C. elegans.
source: Loss-of-function (lf) mutations in smn-1, the C. elegans ortholog of SMN1, cause behavioral and morphological abnormalities, premature death, and sterility (Briese et al., 2009; Sleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in smn-1 cause morphological abnormalities in C. elegans.
source: Loss-of-function (lf) mutations in smn-1, the C. elegans ortholog of SMN1, cause behavioral and morphological abnormalities, premature death, and sterility (Briese et al., 2009; Sleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in smn-1 cause premature death in C. elegans.
source: Loss-of-function (lf) mutations in smn-1, the C. elegans ortholog of SMN1, cause behavioral and morphological abnormalities, premature death, and sterility (Briese et al., 2009; Sleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in smn-1 cause sterility in C. elegans.
source: Loss-of-function (lf) mutations in smn-1, the C. elegans ortholog of SMN1, cause behavioral and morphological abnormalities, premature death, and sterility (Briese et al., 2009; Sleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: smn-1(lf) animals have neuromuscular junction (NMJ) defects.
source: smn-1(lf) animals also have neuromuscular junction (NMJ) defects, suggesting a functional role for SMN-1 in MNs (Briese et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: MNs in smn-1(lf) animals do not die, likely because of their short lifespan.
source: MNs in smn-1(lf) animals do not die, likely because of their short lifespan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C. elegans have a short lifespan and motor neurons do not degenerate in smn-1(lf) animals.

claim: smn-1(lf) neuromuscular defects may correspond to the early stages of SMA pathogenesis.
source: However, smn-1(lf) neuromuscular defects may correspond to the early stages of SMA pathogenesis, characterized by NMJ dysfunction prior to MN degeneration (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by cited references about early SMA pathogenesis.

claim: Early stages of SMA pathogenesis are characterized by NMJ dysfunction prior to MN degeneration.
source: However, smn-1(lf) neuromuscular defects may correspond to the early stages of SMA pathogenesis, characterized by NMJ dysfunction prior to MN degeneration (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The C. elegans Gemin3 ortholog is MEL-46.
source: We find that the C. elegans Gemin3 ortholog, MEL-46, is perturbed by SMN-1 loss, impacting miR-2 suppression of the M2 muscarinic receptor ortholog, GAR-2 (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: MEL-46 is perturbed by SMN-1 loss.
source: We find that the C. elegans Gemin3 ortholog, MEL-46, is perturbed by SMN-1 loss, impacting miR-2 suppression of the M2 muscarinic receptor ortholog, GAR-2 (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing MEL-46 mislocalization in smn-1(ok355) animals in Figure 2.

claim: SMN-1 loss impacts miR-2 suppression of GAR-2.
source: We find that the C. elegans Gemin3 ortholog, MEL-46, is perturbed by SMN-1 loss, impacting miR-2 suppression of the M2 muscarinic receptor ortholog, GAR-2 (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP reporter data and miR-2 level measurements in Figure 5.

claim: miR-128 is a potential miR-2 ortholog.
source: Across species in SMA mouse models, we find decreased levels of miR-128, a potential miR-2 ortholog, and increased expression of the GAR-2 ortholog, m2R.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and functional similarity shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In SMA mouse models, there are decreased levels of miR-128.
source: Across species in SMA mouse models, we find decreased levels of miR-128, a potential miR-2 ortholog, and increased expression of the GAR-2 ortholog, m2R.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In SMA mouse models, there is increased expression of m2R.
source: Across species in SMA mouse models, we find decreased levels of miR-128, a potential miR-2 ortholog, and increased expression of the GAR-2 ortholog, m2R.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: m2R inhibition ameliorates axon outgrowth defects in MNs from a SMA mouse model.
source: Notably, m2R inhibition ameliorates axon outgrowth defects in MNs from a SMA mouse model, consistent with our results in C. elegans.
evidence: This is demonstrated by methoctramine treatment experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: mel-46(tm1739) homozygous loss of function animals had severely decreased pharyngeal pumping rates.
source: Like smn-1 loss in L4 stage animals, we found that mel-46(tm1739) homozygous loss of function animals had severely decreased pharyngeal pumping rates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pharyngeal pumping was restored to normal rates in mel-46(tm1739) animals using a broadly expressed mel-46 rescue array.
source: Pharyngeal pumping was restored to normal rates in mel-46(tm1739) animals using a previously described, broadly expressed mel-46 rescue array (also referred to as [mel-46(+)#1]), which utilizes the mel-46 promoter (Figure 1A) (Minasaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: mel-46 partial loss of function alleles, yt5 and ok3760, caused pumping defects.
source: mel-46 partial loss of function alleles, yt5 and ok3760, also caused pumping defects as did global mel-46 RNA interference (RNAi) or cholinergic neuron-specific mel-46(RNAi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Global mel-46 RNA interference (RNAi) caused pumping defects.
source: mel-46 partial loss of function alleles, yt5 and ok3760, also caused pumping defects as did global mel-46 RNA interference (RNAi) or cholinergic neuron-specific mel-46(RNAi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cholinergic neuron-specific mel-46(RNAi) caused pumping defects.
source: mel-46 partial loss of function alleles, yt5 and ok3760, also caused pumping defects as did global mel-46 RNA interference (RNAi) or cholinergic neuron-specific mel-46(RNAi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MEL-46 is necessary for normal neuromuscular function.
source: We conclude that MEL-46 is necessary for normal neuromuscular function.
evidence: This is inferred from the pumping defects observed in multiple mel-46 loss of function conditions.

claim: mel-46(tm1739) animals paralyzed more slowly when exposed to aldicarb.
source: mel-46(tm1739) animals paralyzed more slowly when exposed to aldicarb, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reintroduction of mel-46 restored normal aldicarb sensitivity in mel-46(tm1739) animals.
source: Reintroduction of mel-46 restored normal aldicarb sensitivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mel-46 loss of function resulted in aldicarb resistance across multiple alleles.
source: We tested if a decrease in MEL-46 function causes similar resistance to aldicarb and found that mel-46 loss of function resulted in aldicarb resistance across multiple alleles (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G), reminiscent of smn-1 loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Tissue-specific knock-down of mel-46 in cholinergic neurons resulted in aldicarb resistance.
source: Tissue-specific knock-down of mel-46 in cholinergic neurons resulted in aldicarb resistance, thus confirming that MEL-46 function is required in cholinergic neurons, as is SMN-1 (Figure 1C) (Dimitriadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MEL-46 function is required in cholinergic neurons.
source: Tissue-specific knock-down of mel-46 in cholinergic neurons resulted in aldicarb resistance, thus confirming that MEL-46 function is required in cholinergic neurons, as is SMN-1 (Figure 1C) (Dimitriadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the aldicarb resistance observed with cholinergic-specific mel-46 knockdown.

claim: Knock-down of mel-46 in inhibitory GABAergic neurons resulted in aldicarb hypersensitivity.
source: We also showed that knock-down of mel-46 or smn-1 in inhibitory GABAergic neurons resulted in aldicarb hypersensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Knock-down of smn-1 in inhibitory GABAergic neurons resulted in aldicarb hypersensitivity.
source: We also showed that knock-down of mel-46 or smn-1 in inhibitory GABAergic neurons resulted in aldicarb hypersensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: MEL-46 is required in both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons for normal NMJ function.
source: Our findings, taken together with previous work, suggest that MEL-46 and SMN-1 are required in both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons for normal NMJ function.
evidence: This is inferred from the aldicarb response data in different neuron types.

claim: SMN-1 is required in both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons for normal NMJ function.
source: Our findings, taken together with previous work, suggest that MEL-46 and SMN-1 are required in both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons for normal NMJ function.
evidence: This is inferred from the aldicarb response data in different neuron types and cited previous work.

claim: Loss of smn-1 results in similar SNB-1 synaptic localization defects as loss of mel-46.
source: Loss of smn-1 or mel-46 resulted in similar SNB-1 synaptic localization defects: decreased SNB-1 puncta width, intensity and linear density (Figure 1D–G) (Dimitriadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 1D-G and cited reference.

claim: Loss of smn-1 leads to decreased APT-4 puncta width and intensity, but increased linear density.
source: Loss of smn-1 leads to decreased APT-4 puncta width and intensity, but increased linear density (Dimitriadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: mel-46(tm1739) animals had increased APT-4 linear density.
source: mel-46(tm1739) animals also had increased APT-4 linear density, but no changes in puncta width or intensity compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: mel-46(tm1739) animals had no changes in APT-4 puncta width or intensity compared to controls.
source: mel-46(tm1739) animals also had increased APT-4 linear density, but no changes in puncta width or intensity compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Decreased mel-46 causes synaptic protein defects that overlap partially with defects observed when SMN-1 levels decrease.
source: Therefore, decreased mel-46 causes synaptic protein defects that overlap partially with defects observed when SMN-1 levels decrease.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of synaptic protein localization defects in mel-46 and smn-1 loss of function animals.

claim: MEL-46::GFP localizes to small granular structures in dorsal cord processes in control and smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: We found that MEL-46::GFP localizes to small granular structures in dorsal cord processes in control (smn-1(+)) and smn-1(ok355) animals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gemin3 localizes to granular structures in mammalian neurites.
source: Our finding is consistent with previous work showing that Gemin3 localizes to granular structures in mammalian neurites; Gemin3 co-localizes with SMN in 50–60% of these granules, along with multiple mRNAs (Todd et al., 2010a, 2010b; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Gemin3 co-localizes with SMN in 50–60% of granular structures in mammalian neurites.
source: Our finding is consistent with previous work showing that Gemin3 localizes to granular structures in mammalian neurites; Gemin3 co-localizes with SMN in 50–60% of these granules, along with multiple mRNAs (Todd et al., 2010a, 2010b; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In smn-1(ok355) animals, the density of MEL-46::GFP-positive granular structures was doubled compared to smn-1(+) controls.
source: In smn-1(ok355) animals, we found that the density of MEL-46::GFP-positive granular structures was doubled compared to smn-1(+) controls (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The mean intensity of MEL-46::GFP fluorescence was decreased in smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: Furthermore, the mean intensity of MEL-46::GFP fluorescence and the maximum fluorescence for each sample were decreased in smn-1(ok355) animals (Figure 2B–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The maximum fluorescence of MEL-46::GFP for each sample was decreased in smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: Furthermore, the mean intensity of MEL-46::GFP fluorescence and the maximum fluorescence for each sample were decreased in smn-1(ok355) animals (Figure 2B–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Decreased SMN-1 leads to MEL-46 mislocalization in cholinergic MN processes.
source: These results suggest that decreased SMN-1 leads to MEL-46 mislocalization in cholinergic MN processes and diminished MEL-46 levels in granules.
evidence: This is inferred from the MEL-46::GFP localization data in smn-1(ok355) animals.

claim: Decreased SMN-1 leads to diminished MEL-46 levels in granules.
source: These results suggest that decreased SMN-1 leads to MEL-46 mislocalization in cholinergic MN processes and diminished MEL-46 levels in granules.
evidence: This is inferred from the MEL-46::GFP intensity data in smn-1(ok355) animals.

claim: Increasing mel-46 gene dosage in smn-1(ok355) animals ameliorated smn-1(ok355) aldicarb resistance defects.
source: To test this hypothesis, we increased mel-46 gene dosage in smn-1(ok355) animals using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array and showed that this ameliorated smn-1(ok355) aldicarb resistance defects (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increasing mel-46 specifically in cholinergic neurons rescued smn-1(ok355) aldicarb resistance.
source: We also showed that increasing mel-46 specifically in cholinergic neurons, using the cholinergic-specific unc-17 (ACh) promoter in an integrated array, referred to as [ACh::mel-46::GFP], rescued smn-1(ok355) aldicarb resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Loss of SMN-1 negatively impacts MEL-46 function, resulting in perturbed NMJ signaling.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that loss of SMN-1 negatively impacts MEL-46 function, resulting in perturbed NMJ signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the MEL-46 mislocalization data and the rescue of NMJ defects by MEL-46 overexpression.

claim: Reduced human SMN levels result in Gemin3 downregulation.
source: Our finding is consistent with observations in humans that reduced human SMN levels result in Gemin3 downregulation (Feng et al., 2005; Helmken et al., 2003),
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Increasing mel-46 did not ameliorate pharyngeal pumping rate defects in smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: For example, pharyngeal pumping rate defects were not ameliorated in smn-1(ok355) animals by increased mel-46 levels ([mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting a privileged relationship between SMN-1 and MEL-46 in cholinergic NMJ signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharyngeal pumping data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Increasing mel-46 rescued smn-1(ok355) synaptic protein localization defects.
source: Increasing mel-46 did rescue smn-1(ok355) synaptic protein localization defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 2F-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, smn-1(ok355) defective SNB-1 puncta width was rescued to normal levels.
source: Using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, we rescued smn-1(ok355) defective SNB-1 puncta width and intensity to normal levels, but did not ameliorate linear density defects (Figure 2F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: Using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, smn-1(ok355) defective SNB-1 puncta intensity was rescued to normal levels.
source: Using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, we rescued smn-1(ok355) defective SNB-1 puncta width and intensity to normal levels, but did not ameliorate linear density defects (Figure 2F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: Using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, smn-1(ok355) SNB-1 puncta linear density defects were not ameliorated.
source: Using the [mel-46(+)#1] rescue array, we rescued smn-1(ok355) defective SNB-1 puncta width and intensity to normal levels, but did not ameliorate linear density defects (Figure 2F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: Increased mel-46 in an smn-1(+) control background did not increase SNB-1 levels.
source: Notably, increased mel-46 in an smn-1(+) control background did not increase SNB-1 levels, suggesting that mel-46-induced up-regulation of SNB-1 is specifically beneficial in a smn-1(ok355) background.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: mel-46-induced up-regulation of SNB-1 is specifically beneficial in a smn-1(ok355) background.
source: Notably, increased mel-46 in an smn-1(+) control background did not increase SNB-1 levels, suggesting that mel-46-induced up-regulation of SNB-1 is specifically beneficial in a smn-1(ok355) background.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mel-46 overexpression rescues SNB-1 defects in smn-1(ok355) but does not increase SNB-1 in wild type.

claim: Increasing mel-46 with a second broadly-expressed mel-46 rescue array line restored APT-4 puncta linear density to normal levels in smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: Increasing mel-46 with a second broadly-expressed mel-46 rescue array line, [mel-46(+)#2], also restored APT-4 puncta linear density to normal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), without rescuing other metrics.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Increasing mel-46 improves neuromuscular signaling in smn-1(ok355) animals by partially restoring levels and localization of synaptic proteins.
source: These results are consistent with the aldicarb/NMJ functional rescue studies presented here and suggest increasing mel-46 improves neuromuscular signaling in smn-1(ok355) animals by partially restoring levels and localization of synaptic proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined aldicarb and synaptic protein localization data.

claim: mel-46 may act with or downstream of smn-1 in a pathway essential for NMJ function.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that mel-46 may act with or downstream of smn-1 in a pathway essential for NMJ function.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing mel-46 overexpression rescues smn-1 defects.

claim: Mammalian Gemin3 directly binds SMN.
source: Since mammalian Gemin3 directly binds SMN (Charroux et al., 1999), increasing MEL-46 (Gemin3) might decrease the rate of SMN-1 loss.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Increasing mel-46 using the [mel-46(+)#2] rescue array did not increase GFP::SMN-1 levels, but caused a modest overall decrease.
source: We found that increasing mel-46 using the [mel-46(+)#2] rescue array did not increase GFP::SMN-1 levels, but unexpectedly caused a modest overall decrease (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: It is unlikely that smn-1(ok355) rescue by increased mel-46 is due to stabilization of maternally-loaded SMN-1.
source: It therefore seems unlikely that smn-1(ok355) rescue by increased mel-46 is due to stabilization of maternally-loaded SMN-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mel-46 overexpression decreases rather than increases GFP::SMN-1 levels.

claim: miR-2 is enriched in neurons.
source: miRNA miR-2 is enriched in neurons, expressed at all developmental stages, and predicted to regulate expression of many proteins involved in neuronal development and function (Marco et al., 2012; Martinez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: miR-2 is expressed at all developmental stages.
source: miRNA miR-2 is enriched in neurons, expressed at all developmental stages, and predicted to regulate expression of many proteins involved in neuronal development and function (Marco et al., 2012; Martinez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: miR-2 is predicted to regulate expression of many proteins involved in neuronal development and function.
source: miRNA miR-2 is enriched in neurons, expressed at all developmental stages, and predicted to regulate expression of many proteins involved in neuronal development and function (Marco et al., 2012; Martinez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Two different mir-2 deletion alleles, gk259 and n4108, caused resistance to aldicarb paralysis compared to wild type animals.
source: Two different deletion alleles, gk259 and n4108, caused resistance to aldicarb paralysis compared to wild type animals (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aldicarb resistance in mir-2(gk259) animals was partially rescued by expressing miR-2 under the control of a cholinergic neuron-specific promoter.
source: This defect was partially rescued by expressing miR-2 under the control of a the unc-17 (ACh) cholinergic neuron-specific promoter (referred to as ([ACh::mir-2(+)]) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loss of miR-2 resulted in a mild pharyngeal pumping defect.
source: Loss of miR-2 also resulted in a mild pharyngeal pumping defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharyngeal pumping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: miR-2 is required in cholinergic neurons for proper NMJ signaling.
source: Taken together, we conclude that miR-2 is required in cholinergic neurons for proper NMJ signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the aldicarb resistance and rescue data.

claim: mir-2(gk259) animals had increased SNB-1 puncta linear density.
source: Analysis of tagged SNB-1 in mir-2(gk259) animals revealed increased SNB-1 puncta linear density, but no change in puncta width or intensity compared to wild type animals (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: mir-2(gk259) animals had no change in SNB-1 puncta width or intensity compared to wild type animals.
source: Analysis of tagged SNB-1 in mir-2(gk259) animals revealed increased SNB-1 puncta linear density, but no change in puncta width or intensity compared to wild type animals (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: mir-2(gk259) animals were indistinguishable from wild type control animals with respect to SYD-2 synaptic localization for all metrics analyzed.
source: Additionally, mir-2(gk259) animals were indistinguishable from wild type control animals with respect to SYD-2 synaptic localization for all metrics analyzed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that pre-synaptic active zones are unchanged in number and size; thus, synaptic changes are likely not the result of altered active zone number or size (Zhen and Jin, 1999).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pre-synaptic active zones are unchanged in number and size in mir-2(gk259) animals.
source: Additionally, mir-2(gk259) animals were indistinguishable from wild type control animals with respect to SYD-2 synaptic localization for all metrics analyzed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that pre-synaptic active zones are unchanged in number and size; thus, synaptic changes are likely not the result of altered active zone number or size (Zhen and Jin, 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the SYD-2 localization data and cited reference.

claim: Synaptic changes in mir-2(gk259) animals are likely not the result of altered active zone number or size.
source: Additionally, mir-2(gk259) animals were indistinguishable from wild type control animals with respect to SYD-2 synaptic localization for all metrics analyzed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that pre-synaptic active zones are unchanged in number and size; thus, synaptic changes are likely not the result of altered active zone number or size (Zhen and Jin, 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the SYD-2 localization data.

claim: ITSN-1 puncta width was decreased in mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108) animals compared to wild type controls.
source: ITSN-1 puncta width and intensity, but not linear density, were decreased in mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108), animals compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: ITSN-1 puncta intensity was decreased in mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108) animals compared to wild type controls.
source: ITSN-1 puncta width and intensity, but not linear density, were decreased in mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108), animals compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: ITSN-1 puncta linear density was not decreased in mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108) animals compared to wild type controls.
source: ITSN-1 puncta width and intensity, but not linear density, were decreased in mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108), animals compared to wild type controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Both mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108) had decreased APT-4 puncta width, intensity, and linear density.
source: Finally, both mir-2(gk259) and mir-2(n4108) had decreased APT-4 puncta width, intensity, and linear density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: Loss of miR-2 results in synaptic dysfunction at the NMJ.
source: Together with results from aldicarb resistance studies, our results suggest that loss of miR-2 results in synaptic dysfunction at the NMJ, consistent with decreased cholinergic synaptic release (Ch'ng et al., 2008; Sieburth et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined aldicarb and synaptic protein localization data.

claim: There is considerable overlap between synaptic protein localization defects resulting from miR-2 loss with those of smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: Additionally, we observed considerable overlap between synaptic protein localization defects resulting from miR-2 loss with those of smn-1(ok355) animals (Dimitriadi et al., 2016), a finding consistent with miR-2 and SMN-1 acting in partially redundant pathways at the NMJ.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of synaptic protein localization data.

claim: miR-2 and SMN-1 act in partially redundant pathways at the NMJ.
source: Additionally, we observed considerable overlap between synaptic protein localization defects resulting from miR-2 loss with those of smn-1(ok355) animals (Dimitriadi et al., 2016), a finding consistent with miR-2 and SMN-1 acting in partially redundant pathways at the NMJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap in synaptic protein localization defects.

claim: Loss of gar-2(ok520) resulted in the most complete suppression of mir-2(gk259) aldicarb resistance.
source: Loss of any of these four genes suppressed mir-2(gk259) to some extent, but gar-2(ok520), which contains a large deletion removing gar-2 exons 6 and 7, resulted in the most complete suppression, thus suggesting that GAR-2 acts downstream of miR-2 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: GAR-2 acts downstream of miR-2.
source: Loss of any of these four genes suppressed mir-2(gk259) to some extent, but gar-2(ok520), which contains a large deletion removing gar-2 exons 6 and 7, resulted in the most complete suppression, thus suggesting that GAR-2 acts downstream of miR-2 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic suppression data.

claim: GAR-2 is a G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor orthologous to the mammalian M2 muscarinic receptor (m2R).
source: GAR-2 is a G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor orthologous to the mammalian M2 muscarinic receptor (m2R) (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Animals with the scrambled miR-2 binding site (gar-2 UTRscrC) were resistant to aldicarb.
source: Compared to control animals (gar-2 UTRwtC) carrying the disrupted PAM site mutation (C>T), we found that animals with the scrambled miR-2 binding site (gar-2 UTRscrC) were resistant to aldicarb, similar to miR-2 loss (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: gar-2 UTRscrC animals had a 40% increase in gar-2 transcript compared to gar-2 UTRwtC controls.
source: To evaluate whether disruption of the miR-2 binding site influenced gar-2 transcript levels, we compared gar-2 mRNA levels in gar-2 UTRscrC animals and gar-2 UTRwtC controls and found a 40% increase in gar-2 transcript in gar-2 UTRscrC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Increased GFP levels were observed in mir-2(gk259) animals expressing the intact 3'UTR construct as compared to control animals.
source: Increased GFP levels were observed in mir-2(gk259) animals expressing the intact 3'UTR construct as compared to control animals (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Loss of the mir-2 gene did not affect GFP levels in animals expressing the scrambled 3'UTR construct compared to control.
source: Whereas, loss of the mir-2 gene did not affect GFP levels in animals expressing the scrambled 3'UTR construct compared to control (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: There was a ~13% increase in relative GFP expression associated with loss of miR-2.
source: By this method, we observed a ~13% increase in relative GFP expression associated with loss of miR-2 (Figure 4H), indicating that miR-2 directly suppresses translation of gar-2 mRNA by binding the gar-2 3'UTR at this 3'UTR site.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric analysis of GFP reporter data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: miR-2 directly suppresses translation of gar-2 mRNA by binding the gar-2 3'UTR.
source: By this method, we observed a ~13% increase in relative GFP expression associated with loss of miR-2 (Figure 4H), indicating that miR-2 directly suppresses translation of gar-2 mRNA by binding the gar-2 3'UTR at this 3'UTR site.
evidence: This is inferred from the GFP reporter data showing increased expression when miR-2 is lost and the binding site is intact.

claim: There was no significant difference in gar-2 mRNA levels between wild type animals and mir-2(gk259) loss of function animals.
source: We also assessed the effect of miR-2 loss on gar-2 transcript levels and found no significant difference in gar-2 mRNA levels between wild type animals and mir-2(gk259) loss of function animals (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: miR-2 binds and inhibits gar-2 mRNA translation, but does not reduce transcript levels.
source: These results, combined with our reporter data, suggest that miR-2 binds and inhibits gar-2 mRNA translation, but does not reduce transcript levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined GFP reporter and qPCR data.

claim: miRNAs can influence protein synthesis of targets without destabilizing mRNA levels.
source: Previous studies have reported that miRNAs can influence protein synthesis of targets without destabilizing mRNA levels (Cloonan, 2015; Selbach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: There was a small increase in relative GFP reporter expression (~5%) in smn-1(ok355) animals compared to smn-1(+) controls.
source: Using the same ratiometric strategy from Figure 4H, we observed a small increase in relative GFP reporter expression (~5%) in smn-1(ok355) animals compared to smn-1(+) controls (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric analysis of GFP reporter data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: smn-1(ok355) animals may have decreased miR-2 function and increased GAR-2 translation.
source: This finding suggested that smn-1(ok355) animals may have decreased miR-2 function and, as a consequence, an increase in GAR-2 translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the GFP reporter data.

claim: In smn-1(ok355) animals, increasing mel-46 caused decreased relative reporter expression by ~15%, compared to smn-1(ok355) animals lacking the mel-46 rescue array.
source: However, in smn-1(ok355) animals, increasing mel-46 caused decreased relative reporter expression by ~15%, compared to smn-1(ok355) animals lacking the mel-46 rescue array (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric analysis of GFP reporter data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: MEL-46 overexpression decreases GAR-2 levels in smn-1(ok355) by increasing miR-2 activity.
source: These data suggest that MEL-46 overexpression decreases GAR-2 levels in smn-1(ok355) by increasing miR-2 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the GFP reporter data showing decreased expression when mel-46 is overexpressed in smn-1(ok355) background.

claim: After neuron-specific RNAi knock-down of either SMN-1 or MEL-46, there were decreases in mature miR-2 levels.
source: After neuron-specific RNAi knock-down of either SMN-1 or MEL-46, we found decreases in mature miR-2 levels (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), but no change in gar-2 transcript levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: After neuron-specific RNAi knock-down of either SMN-1 or MEL-46, there was no change in gar-2 transcript levels.
source: After neuron-specific RNAi knock-down of either SMN-1 or MEL-46, we found decreases in mature miR-2 levels (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), but no change in gar-2 transcript levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Neuronal miR-2 levels are decreased when MEL-46 or SMN-1 levels decrease.
source: These results suggest neuronal miR-2 levels are decreased when MEL-46 or SMN-1 levels decrease.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing decreased miR-2 after RNAi knockdown.

claim: Diminished SMN-1 leads to decreased miR-2 levels and activity, resulting in increased GAR-2 expression.
source: Collectively, our data above are consistent with a model where diminished SMN-1 leads to decreased miR-2 levels and activity, resulting in increased GAR-2 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined GFP reporter and qPCR data.

claim: M2 receptors inhibit synaptic release at cholinergic NMJs across species.
source: Since M2 receptors inhibit synaptic release at cholinergic NMJs across species (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008; Parnas et al., 2005; Slutsky et al., 2003), overexpression of these receptors in smn-1(ok355) MNs might contribute to the NMJ defects previously observed in these animals (Dimitriadi et al., 2016; Sleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Overexpression of M2 receptors in smn-1(ok355) MNs might contribute to the NMJ defects previously observed in these animals.
source: Since M2 receptors inhibit synaptic release at cholinergic NMJs across species (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008; Parnas et al., 2005; Slutsky et al., 2003), overexpression of these receptors in smn-1(ok355) MNs might contribute to the NMJ defects previously observed in these animals (Dimitriadi et al., 2016; Sleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of M2 receptors and the observed increase in GAR-2 expression.

claim: Increased MEL-46/Gemin3 might have an ameliorative effect in animals lacking SMN-1 by stimulating miR-2 activity, thus decreasing GAR-2 levels and disinhibiting cholinergic release.
source: Furthermore, increased MEL-46/Gemin3 might have an ameliorative effect in animals lacking SMN-1 by stimulating miR-2 activity, thus decreasing GAR-2 levels and disinhibiting cholinergic release.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing mel-46 overexpression rescues smn-1 defects and decreases GAR-2 reporter expression.

claim: Loss of GAR-2 did not improve pharyngeal pumping rates in smn-1(ok355) animals.
source: Loss of GAR-2 did not improve pharyngeal pumping rates in smn-1(ok355) animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), similar to our results in animals with increased mel-46 levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharyngeal pumping data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: gar-2(ok520) restored normal response to aldicarb in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) animals.
source: However, similar to increasing mel-46, gar-2(ok520) restored normal response to aldicarb in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) animals (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), consistent with improved NMJ function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: gar-2(ok520) restored normal response to aldicarb in mel-46(tm1739) animals.
source: Additionally, gar-2(ok520) restored normal response to aldicarb in mel-46(tm1739) animals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aldicarb response assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Decreasing GAR-2 likely improves presynaptic function in animals with decreased SMN-1 or MEL-46.
source: Our results indicate that decreasing GAR-2 likely improves presynaptic function in animals with decreased SMN-1 or MEL-46.
evidence: This is inferred from the aldicarb rescue data.

claim: gar-2(ok520) rescued SNB-1 puncta width defects in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) backgrounds.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, gar-2(ok520) also rescued numerous presynaptic protein localization defects caused by SMN-1 loss; SNB-1 puncta width, intensity and linear density defects were rescued in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) backgrounds (Figure 6C–6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6C-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: gar-2(ok520) rescued SNB-1 puncta intensity defects in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) backgrounds.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, gar-2(ok520) also rescued numerous presynaptic protein localization defects caused by SMN-1 loss; SNB-1 puncta width, intensity and linear density defects were rescued in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) backgrounds (Figure 6C–6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6C-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: gar-2(ok520) rescued SNB-1 puncta linear density defects in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) backgrounds.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, gar-2(ok520) also rescued numerous presynaptic protein localization defects caused by SMN-1 loss; SNB-1 puncta width, intensity and linear density defects were rescued in both smn-1(ok355) and smn-1(rt248) backgrounds (Figure 6C–6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6C-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: GAR-2 loss in smn-1(+) control animals resulted in increased SNB-1 puncta width and intensity.
source: GAR-2 loss in smn-1(+) control animals resulted in increased SNB-1 puncta width and intensity, but did not alter SNB-1 puncta linear density.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6C-G.

claim: GAR-2 loss in smn-1(+) control animals did not alter SNB-1 puncta linear density.
source: GAR-2 loss in smn-1(+) control animals resulted in increased SNB-1 puncta width and intensity, but did not alter SNB-1 puncta linear density.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6C-G.

claim: m2R internalization normally occurs in response to chronic m2R stimulation in vertebrates.
source: Research in vertebrates has demonstrated m2R internalization normally occurs in response to chronic m2R stimulation, either by pharmacological agonist application or acetylcholinesterase inhibition (Clancy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Endocytosis is defective in animals lacking SMN-1.
source: Since endocytosis is defective in animals lacking SMN-1, perturbed endocytosis, in combination with miRNA misregulation, could contribute to GAR-2 accumulation at the membrane leading to decreased SNB-1 in smn-1(ok355) motor neurons (Dimitriadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Perturbed endocytosis, in combination with miRNA misregulation, could contribute to GAR-2 accumulation at the membrane in smn-1(ok355) motor neurons.
source: Since endocytosis is defective in animals lacking SMN-1, perturbed endocytosis, in combination with miRNA misregulation, could contribute to GAR-2 accumulation at the membrane leading to decreased SNB-1 in smn-1(ok355) motor neurons (Dimitriadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known defects in endocytosis and miRNA regulation.

claim: Loss of GAR-2 did not rescue smn-1(ok355) APT-4 puncta defects.
source: Loss of GAR-2 did not rescue smn-1(ok355) APT-4 puncta defects (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), but decreased APT-4 puncta width and intensity in smn-1(+) control animals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of GAR-2 decreased APT-4 puncta width and intensity in smn-1(+) control animals.
source: Loss of GAR-2 did not rescue smn-1(ok355) APT-4 puncta defects (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), but decreased APT-4 puncta width and intensity in smn-1(+) control animals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synaptic protein localization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There are additional pathways affected by smn-1 loss, beyond GAR-2 misregulation.
source: As loss of GAR-2 did not restore APT-4 synaptic defects, we conclude that there are additional pathways affected by smn-1 loss, beyond GAR-2 misregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue of synaptic defects by GAR-2 loss.

claim: C. elegans GAR-2 levels are increased by smn-1 loss.
source: Nevertheless, these results suggest that C. elegans GAR-2 levels are increased by smn-1 loss, which might contribute to NMJ defects in smn-1(lf) animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the GFP reporter data and genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Increased C. elegans GAR-2 levels might contribute to NMJ defects in smn-1(lf) animals.
source: Nevertheless, these results suggest that C. elegans GAR-2 levels are increased by smn-1 loss, which might contribute to NMJ defects in smn-1(lf) animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic rescue experiments showing GAR-2 loss ameliorates smn-1 defects.

claim: The closest human ortholog of GAR-2 is the M2 muscarinic receptor (m2R), encoded by the CHRM2 gene.
source: The closest human ortholog of GAR-2 is the M2 muscarinic receptor (m2R), encoded by the CHRM2 gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on sequence homology.

claim: GAR-2 and m2R are functionally conserved.
source: GAR-2 and m2R are functionally conserved, as activation of these presynaptic receptors by acetylcholine in different species results in hyperpolarization and decreased NMJ acetylcholine release across species (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008; Dudel, 2007; Parnas et al., 2005; Slutsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Activation of GAR-2 and m2R by acetylcholine results in hyperpolarization and decreased NMJ acetylcholine release across species.
source: GAR-2 and m2R are functionally conserved, as activation of these presynaptic receptors by acetylcholine in different species results in hyperpolarization and decreased NMJ acetylcholine release across species (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008; Dudel, 2007; Parnas et al., 2005; Slutsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The CHRM2 mRNA is a predicted target of miR-128 in mice and humans.
source: The CHRM2 mRNA is a predicted target of miR-128 in mice and humans (Figure 7A) (Jan et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2005; Paraskevopoulou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A ~50% increase in m2R levels was observed in MNs isolated from E13.5 SMA mice compared to wild type control MNs.
source: m2R protein levels were examined in MNs isolated from E13.5 SMA mice (Smn-/-;SMN2tg/0). A ~50% increase in m2R levels was observed, compared to wild type control MNs (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: miR-128 levels in SMA mouse MNs were decreased compared to wild type.
source: miR-128 levels in SMA mouse MNs were decreased compared to wild type (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Diminished SMN protein causes decreased levels of mature miR-128 in MNs across species.
source: Combined, these results suggest that diminished SMN protein causes decreased levels of mature miR-128, thus disinhibiting m2R expression in MNs across species.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing decreased miR-128 and increased m2R in SMA mouse MNs.

claim: Diminished SMN protein disinhibits m2R expression in MNs across species.
source: Combined, these results suggest that diminished SMN protein causes decreased levels of mature miR-128, thus disinhibiting m2R expression in MNs across species.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing decreased miR-128 and increased m2R in SMA mouse MNs.

claim: Decreased SMN levels result in axon outgrowth defects in MNs derived from a SMA mouse model.
source: Decreased SMN levels results in axon outgrowth defects in MNs derived from a SMA mouse model (Rossoll et al., 2003) and increased m2R might contribute to this functional defect.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Increased m2R might contribute to axon outgrowth defects in MNs derived from a SMA mouse model.
source: Decreased SMN levels results in axon outgrowth defects in MNs derived from a SMA mouse model (Rossoll et al., 2003) and increased m2R might contribute to this functional defect.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed increase in m2R levels.

claim: In wild type MNs, methoctramine decreased mean longest axon length.
source: In wild type MNs, methoctramine decreased mean longest axon length.
evidence: This is demonstrated by axon length measurements shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Methoctramine treatment in SMA MNs increased mean longest axon length.
source: Conversely, methoctramine treatment in SMA MNs increased both mean longest axon length and total axon length (Figure 7E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by axon length measurements shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Methoctramine treatment in SMA MNs increased total axon length.
source: Conversely, methoctramine treatment in SMA MNs increased both mean longest axon length and total axon length (Figure 7E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by axon length measurements shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: m2R inhibition rescues MN axon outgrowth defects in a SMA mouse model.
source: We conclude that m2R inhibition rescues MN axon outgrowth defects in a SMA mouse model, consistent with a deleterious impact of increased m2R activity in SMA model MNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the methoctramine treatment data.

claim: Increased m2R activity has a deleterious impact in SMA model MNs.
source: We conclude that m2R inhibition rescues MN axon outgrowth defects in a SMA mouse model, consistent with a deleterious impact of increased m2R activity in SMA model MNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of axon outgrowth defects by m2R inhibition.

claim: Many pathways are perturbed by SMN loss, including spliceosome assembly, pre-mRNA splicing, mRNA transport, endocytosis, and axon growth.
source: Many pathways are perturbed by SMN loss, including spliceosome assembly, pre-mRNA splicing, mRNA transport, endocytosis, and axon growth (Dimitriadi et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2011; Hosseinibarkooie et al., 2016; McWhorter et al., 2003; Meister et al., 2001; Pellizzoni et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The human CHRM2 locus lacks introns.
source: As the human CHRM2 locus lacks introns (Gosso et al., 2007), spliceosomal defects caused by SMN1 loss of function are unlikely to directly affect mature CHRM2 mRNA levels, although indirect effects are possible.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Spliceosomal defects caused by SMN1 loss of function are unlikely to directly affect mature CHRM2 mRNA levels.
source: As the human CHRM2 locus lacks introns (Gosso et al., 2007), spliceosomal defects caused by SMN1 loss of function are unlikely to directly affect mature CHRM2 mRNA levels, although indirect effects are possible.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of introns in CHRM2.

claim: The simplest model explaining why SMN loss alters m2R levels is one in which decreased SMN levels impact Gemin3 function, thus perturbing miRNA pathways, including miR-128 suppression of m2R translation.
source: Based on our results, the simplest model explaining why SMN loss alters m2R levels is one in which decreased SMN levels impact Gemin3 function, thus perturbing miRNA pathways, including miR-128 suppression of m2R translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results across C. elegans and mouse models.

claim: m2R up-regulation may contribute to MN defects in early stages of SMA pathogenesis.
source: As m2R receptors inhibit cholinergic MN synaptic release (Slutsky et al., 2003), m2R up-regulation may contribute to MN defects in early stages of SMA pathogenesis, in parallel to perturbation of other pathways affected by SMN loss (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of m2R and the observed increase in m2R levels in SMA models.

claim: Decreases in SMN-1(SMN) or MEL-46(Gemin3) result in similar neuromuscular defects.
source: Results presented here indicate that decreases in SMN-1(SMN) or MEL-46(Gemin3) result in similar neuromuscular defects as well as decreased miR-2 levels in neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the aldicarb, pumping, and synaptic protein localization data in Figures 1-2.

claim: Decreases in SMN-1(SMN) or MEL-46(Gemin3) result in decreased miR-2 levels in neurons.
source: Results presented here indicate that decreases in SMN-1(SMN) or MEL-46(Gemin3) result in similar neuromuscular defects as well as decreased miR-2 levels in neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data in Figure 5B.

claim: Decreases in C. elegans SMN-1 result in increased GAR-2 (m2R) through miR-2 misregulation.
source: This analysis further suggests that decreases in C. elegans SMN-1 result in increased GAR-2 (m2R) through miR-2 misregulation and that increasing MEL-46 (Gemin3) reduces GAR-2 protein levels in smn-1(ok355) animals via modulation of miR-2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP reporter data in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing MEL-46 (Gemin3) reduces GAR-2 protein levels in smn-1(ok355) animals via modulation of miR-2.
source: This analysis further suggests that decreases in C. elegans SMN-1 result in increased GAR-2 (m2R) through miR-2 misregulation and that increasing MEL-46 (Gemin3) reduces GAR-2 protein levels in smn-1(ok355) animals via modulation of miR-2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP reporter data in Figure 5A.

claim: Decreased and/or mislocalized Gemin3 may impair RISC function, leading to diminished miR-2 activity and levels.
source: It is possible that decreased and/or mislocalized Gemin3 impairs RISC function, leading to the diminished miR-2 activity and levels reported in Figure 5.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known association of Gemin3 with RISC components.

claim: Gemin3 likely functions in numerous pathways.
source: However, since Gemin3 likely functions in numerous pathways, it may influence miR-2 through other, more indirect pathways.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Gemin3 function.

claim: Gemin3 may influence miR-2 through indirect pathways.
source: However, since Gemin3 likely functions in numerous pathways, it may influence miR-2 through other, more indirect pathways.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: In Drosophila, Gemin3 is necessary for motor function.
source: In Drosophila, Gemin3 is necessary for motor function, but the molecular mechanisms underlying this defect are unclear (Cauchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Results in C. elegans support a requirement for Gemin3 in motor function.
source: Results presented here in C. elegans further support a requirement for Gemin3 in motor function and additionally, show that Gemin3 is capable of modifying miRNA levels and activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mel-46 loss of function and rescue data in Figures 1-2.

claim: Gemin3 is capable of modifying miRNA levels and activity.
source: Results presented here in C. elegans further support a requirement for Gemin3 in motor function and additionally, show that Gemin3 is capable of modifying miRNA levels and activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the miR-2 level and GFP reporter data in Figure 5.

claim: miR-2 belongs to the invertebrate K box family (motif: CUGUGAUA) of miRNAs.
source: miR-2 belongs to the invertebrate K box family (motif: CUGUGAUA) of miRNAs (Ibáñez-Ventoso et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: It was suggested that miR-2 does not have well-conserved mammalian orthologs.
source: It was suggested previously that miR-2 does not have well-conserved mammalian orthologs (Marco et al., 2012), but another study suggested that human miR-128 is a member of this miRNA family (Ibáñez-Ventoso et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Another study suggested that human miR-128 is a member of the K box miRNA family.
source: It was suggested previously that miR-2 does not have well-conserved mammalian orthologs (Marco et al., 2012), but another study suggested that human miR-128 is a member of this miRNA family (Ibáñez-Ventoso et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The CUGUG seed region may be a conserved motif for miRNA binding between miR-2 and miR-128.
source: Our alignment of miR-2/miR-128 miRNAs and gar-2/CHRM2 mRNAs suggests that the CUGUG seed region may be a conserved motif for miRNA binding (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Both miR-2 and miR-128 are enriched in the nervous system.
source: Both miR-2 and miR-128 are enriched in the nervous system and share conserved mRNA targets (Marco et al., 2012; Martinez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: miR-2 and miR-128 share conserved mRNA targets.
source: Both miR-2 and miR-128 are enriched in the nervous system and share conserved mRNA targets (Marco et al., 2012; Martinez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Overall miRNA misregulation contributes to neuronal defects when SMN levels decrease.
source: Regardless, the results presented here, in conjunction with previous research, suggest that overall miRNA misregulation contributes to neuronal defects when SMN levels decrease (Haramati et al., 2010; Kye et al., 2014; Valsecchi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014; Wertz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results and cited references.

claim: Altered function of miR-2/miR-128 or GAR-2/m2R is not sufficient to explain all of the dysfunction observed in models of SMN deficiency.
source: Altered function of miR-2/miR-128 or GAR-2/m2R is not sufficient to explain all of the dysfunction observed in models of SMN deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue of defects by GAR-2 loss and the presence of other affected pathways.

claim: In C. elegans, miR-2 loss does not cause overt defects.
source: In C. elegans, miR-2 loss does not cause overt defects and GAR-2 loss does not restore viability, fecundity, or normal development to animals lacking SMN-1 or MEL-46.
evidence: This is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: GAR-2 loss does not restore viability, fecundity, or normal development to animals lacking SMN-1 or MEL-46.
source: In C. elegans, miR-2 loss does not cause overt defects and GAR-2 loss does not restore viability, fecundity, or normal development to animals lacking SMN-1 or MEL-46.
evidence: This is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: miR-2 loss does not contribute to defects outside the NMJ caused by SMN-1 loss.
source: This suggests miR-2 loss does not contribute to defects outside the NMJ caused by SMN-1 loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that miR-2 loss does not cause overt defects.

claim: Synaptic protein perturbations are more severe in animals with diminished SMN-1 or MEL-46, compared to those lacking either miR-2 or GAR-2.
source: And, at the NMJ, synaptic protein perturbations are more severe in animals with diminished SMN-1 or MEL-46, compared to those lacking either miR-2 or GAR-2, which is consistent with a broader range of defects caused by decreased SMN-1 levels.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of synaptic protein localization data across different genotypes.

claim: Complete miR-128 knock-out results in decreased motor activity and premature death in mice.
source: In mice, complete miR-128 knock-out results in decreased motor activity and premature death (Tan et al., 2013), but it is currently unknown how miR-128 loss might specifically impact cholinergic MN function.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: It is currently unknown how miR-128 loss might specifically impact cholinergic MN function.
source: In mice, complete miR-128 knock-out results in decreased motor activity and premature death (Tan et al., 2013), but it is currently unknown how miR-128 loss might specifically impact cholinergic MN function.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: m2R levels were increased 50% overall in SMN-deficient mouse MNs compared to wild type by Western blot analysis.
source: We found that m2R levels were increased 50% overall in SMN-deficient mouse MNs compared to wild type by Western blot analysis (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: In C. elegans, relative GAR-2 translation was increased by only 5% globally when SMN-1 levels dropped, based on GFP reporter expression in cholinergic neurons.
source: In C. elegans, relative GAR-2 translation was increased by only 5% globally when SMN-1 levels dropped, based on GFP reporter expression in cholinergic neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The C. elegans experiment only investigated the contribution of miR-2 perturbation in regards to increased GAR-2 translation.
source: These two assays are not directly comparable, since the C. elegans experiment only investigated the contribution of miR-2 perturbation in regards to increased GAR-2 translation.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Additional pathways are affected by SMN loss, beyond miRNAs, contributing to the greatly increased m2R levels in SMN-deficient MNs.
source: Certainly, additional pathways are affected by SMN loss, beyond miRNAs, contributing to the greatly increased m2R levels in SMN-deficient MNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in magnitude of m2R increase between C. elegans and mouse models.

claim: These pathways may include mRNA transport metabolism, endocytosis, as well as spliceosome and ribonucleoprotein assembly.
source: These pathways may include mRNA transport metabolism, endocytosis, as well as spliceosome and ribonucleoprotein assembly (Dimitriadi et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2011; Hosseinibarkooie et al., 2016; Pellizzoni et al., 2002; Yong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: m2R is expressed in α-MNs.
source: m2R is expressed in α-MNs, with little to no expression in smaller gamma MNs (Welton et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: m2R has little to no expression in smaller gamma MNs.
source: m2R is expressed in α-MNs, with little to no expression in smaller gamma MNs (Welton et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: m2R expression profile correlates with the pattern of neurodegeneration in an SMA mouse model: selective loss of α-MNs, while gamma MNs remain unaffected.
source: This expression profile correlates with the pattern of neurodegeneration in an SMA mouse model: selective loss of α-MNs, while gamma MNs remain unaffected (Powis and Gillingwater, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Within α-MNs, m2R is distributed along the membrane and concentrates at postsynaptic connections with C-boutons.
source: Within α-MNs, m2R is distributed along the membrane and concentrates at postsynaptic connections with C-boutons (Deardorff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: α-MNs in SMNΔ7 mice have increased C-bouton sites.
source: α-MNs in SMNΔ7 mice have increased C-bouton sites (Tarabal et al., 2014), which could be an additional cause or consequence of increased m2R levels in α-MNs.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Increased C-bouton sites could be an additional cause or consequence of increased m2R levels in α-MNs.
source: α-MNs in SMNΔ7 mice have increased C-bouton sites (Tarabal et al., 2014), which could be an additional cause or consequence of increased m2R levels in α-MNs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: Increased m2R is consistent with multiple features of SMA pathology.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests that increased m2R is consistent with multiple features of SMA pathology.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between m2R expression and neurodegeneration patterns.

claim: m2R receptor activation leads to GIRK-channel-dependent efflux of K+ cations, resulting in neuronal hyperpolarization and decreased SV release.
source: Classically, m2R receptor activation leads to GIRK-channel-dependent efflux of K+ cations, resulting in neuronal hyperpolarization and decreased SV release (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Increased m2R levels are consistent with the synaptic defects observed in SMA models across species.
source: Therefore, increased m2R levels are consistent with the synaptic defects observed in SMA models across species (Dimitriadi et al., 2016; Kong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of m2R and cited references.

claim: m2R activation of GIRK channels is conserved in C. elegans.
source: m2R activation of GIRK channels is conserved in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2000), suggesting GAR-2 loss may rescue NMJ defects in animals lacking SMN-1 by reducing GIRK channel activation.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: GAR-2 loss may rescue NMJ defects in animals lacking SMN-1 by reducing GIRK channel activation.
source: m2R activation of GIRK channels is conserved in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2000), suggesting GAR-2 loss may rescue NMJ defects in animals lacking SMN-1 by reducing GIRK channel activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known function of GAR-2.

claim: Sustained GIRK activation has been previously linked to neurodegeneration.
source: Interestingly, sustained GIRK activation has been previously linked to neurodegeneration (Coulson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: m2R inhibits N-type Ca2+ (Cav2.2) and P/Q-type Ca2+ (Cav2.1) channels resulting in decreased SV release at the NMJ.
source: m2R inhibits N-type Ca2+ (Cav2.2) and P/Q-type Ca2+ (Cav2.1) channels resulting in decreased SV release at the NMJ (Slutsky et al., 2003; Yan and Surmeier, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.
